REASONING:
Step 1 – Frame the project  
- Objective: Deliver free breakfast clubs (FBC) in all state‑funded primary schools in England, providing food and ≥30 min supervised childcare before school.  
- Scope: National rollout year 1 (April 2026‑March 2027) adding ~2,000 schools (500 in Cohort 1, 1,750 in Cohort 2) to the existing 750 early‑adopter (EA) schools.  
- Components: Funding grants (start‑up £1,000, daily £25 + £1 per child), hybrid internal/external delivery, CRM system, call‑centre pilot, advisory support via the education & children’s social care framework, local‑authority assistance.  
- Delivery model: Section 14 grants to schools; internal CRM development; contracted advisers; optional call‑centre.  
- Timeline: CRM MVP by Nov 2025; Cohort 1 start Apr 2026; NSBP closure Jul 2026; Cohort 2 start Sep 2026; evaluation 2026‑2028.  
- Budget: Funded from the Best Start in Life budget; £1,000 start‑up + variable daily rates; overall affordable for up to 2,250 schools.  
- Key stakeholders: Department for Education (DfE), senior responsible officer (SRO) & project board, HM Treasury, schools, local authorities, sector partners, advisers, pupils/parents, evaluation team.  
- External dependencies: Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Bill (legislative duty), closure of the National School Breakfast Programme (NSBP), labour‑market cost adjustments, procurement processes.

Step 2 – Category sweep (candidate risks with supporting text)  
Technical  
1. CRM system may not be ready on time – “We will develop a customer relationship management system internally, working towards a minimum‑viable product from November 2025.”  
2. Call‑centre pilot may encounter implementation problems – “We will also start commercial processes to begin a call‑centre pilot to support data collection.”  
3. Food‑standards compliance risk – “Food provided must be in line with school food standards.”  

Financial  
4. Delay in HM Treasury budget approval – “The programme's success depends on timely approval and budget confirmation from HM Treasury.”  
5. Uncertainty of funding for future years – “Funding for future years will be agreed separately through business cases.”  

Schedule  
6. Cohort 1 start‑up could slip – “Cohort 1 will begin delivery in April 2026.”  
7. Transition from NSBP may be mistimed – “All schools … would be guaranteed a place … after the closure of the NSBP in July 2026.”  

Stakeholder  
8. Low uptake of school applications – “Schools with 40 % or more FSM … will be eligible to apply for a place.”  
9. Local‑authority capacity to support schools – “We will fund local authorities to support schools and the wider system to effectively deliver free breakfast clubs.”  
10. Insufficient collaboration with sector partners – “The programme's success depends on … effective collaboration with the sector partners …”  

Political/Regulatory  
11. Delay in the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Bill – “Children's Wellbeing and Schools Bill will place a duty on state‑funded schools to offer a breakfast club.”  
12. Food‑standards compliance (also political) – same as risk 3.  

Organizational  
13. Availability of skilled staff – “availability of skilled staff and resources, in both DfE and the education sector.”  
14. Governance bottlenecks – “Programme governance is multi‑layered, with primary oversight at the senior responsible officer (SRO) led ‘free breakfast clubs project board’.”  

External  
15. Area cost adjustments may misalign funding – “Across all settings, we apply an area cost adjustment to the funding to account for variations in the labour market.”  

Step 3 – Evidence filter  
All listed risks are directly supported by quoted statements; no risk is removed.

Step 4 – Assess & Mitigate (likelihood 1‑5, impact 1‑5)  

| ID | Likelihood | Impact | Justification | Mitigation |
|----|------------|--------|---------------|------------|
| R01 | 3 | 4 | Internal software projects often face schedule slips. | Set a detailed development plan, allocate dedicated team, conduct early user testing, and prepare a manual onboarding fallback. |
| R02 | 3 | 3 | New commercial process; pilot may encounter technical or staffing issues. | Pilot with limited scope, define clear SOPs, and retain alternative data‑submission methods (e.g., spreadsheet upload). |
| R03 | 2 | 4 | Schools are accustomed to standards, but breach would be regulatory. | Issue clear guidance, provide compliance checklists, and conduct periodic audits/training. |
| R04 | 3 | 5 | Funding delay would halt grant payments and rollout. | Early engagement with Treasury, submit detailed business case, secure provisional approval, and maintain contingency cash reserves. |
| R05 | 3 | 4 | Future‑year funding not guaranteed could threaten sustainability. | Develop a multi‑year funding roadmap, demonstrate early benefits, align with Treasury priorities, and explore alternative financing. |
| R06 | 2 | 4 | Start‑up delay would push the whole schedule. | Create a detailed rollout checklist, monitor readiness weekly, and allocate contingency resources to meet the April 2026 target. |
| R07 | 2 | 3 | Mis‑alignment with NSBP closure could leave a provision gap. | Align transition timelines, provide bridge funding for July‑Sept 2026, and communicate clearly with affected schools. |
| R08 | 3 | 3 | Application eligibility may limit number of schools joining. | Run targeted outreach, simplify application process, and offer incentives (e.g., priority support). |
| R09 | 3 | 3 | Local authorities may lack capacity to deliver support. | Provide training, dedicated support staff, and monitor workload through regular reporting. |
| R10 | 3 | 3 | Poor collaboration could impede delivery of advisory services. | Formal partnership agreements, regular coordination meetings, and shared performance metrics. |
| R11 | 2 | 5 | If the Bill is delayed, the statutory duty is absent. | Track legislative progress, engage MPs, and prepare interim guidance for schools. |
| R12 | 3 | 3 | Skilled staff shortages could affect programme operations. | Recruit temporary staff, cross‑train existing personnel, and offer incentives for retention. |
| R13 | 2 | 3 | Multi‑layered governance may slow decisions. | Streamline decision pathways, define clear escalation routes, and set decision‑making time‑boxes. |
| R14 | 2 | 2 | Labour‑market cost variations could cause funding mismatches. | Review area adjustments annually and adjust grant rates accordingly. |

Step 5 – Consolidate  
Risk 3 (food‑standards) is retained under political_regulatory; duplicate removed. Final set: 14 risks.
